title: Trials, Ethics and Hidden Harms
summary: Learn how modern clinical trials and safety science grew out of landmark studies, ethical failures and unexpected toxicities.

lessons.title: The 1948 MRC Streptomycin Trial: The First Modern RCT

levels.kid:
Long ago, an illness called **tuberculosis** (TB) hurt people's lungs. Many young people died from it. Then a new medicine called **streptomycin** arrived. It was made by tiny germs that live in soil.

But Britain had only a little of it. There was not enough for everyone! So scientists asked a smart question: does this medicine really work?

They picked who got the medicine by **chance**, like pulling names from a hat. That way, nobody could choose only the strongest patients. One group got the medicine plus bed rest. The other group got bed rest alone.

The medicine group did much better, and fewer of them died. But in some people, the TB germs learned to fight back against the medicine. Later, scientists fixed this by giving two medicines together.
levels.hs:
In 1948 the British Medical Journal published a study that many historians call the first modern **randomized controlled trial (RCT)**. It was the Medical Research Council's (MRC's) test of **streptomycin** for **pulmonary tuberculosis**, meaning TB of the lungs.

Streptomycin was discovered in 1943 by Albert Schatz, a student in Selman Waksman's lab at Rutgers University. It came from the soil bacterium Streptomyces griseus and was the first antibiotic that worked against TB. Post-war Britain could afford only a small supply.

The statistician **Austin Bradford Hill** turned that shortage into an opportunity. There wasn't enough drug for everyone anyway, so it was fair to let chance decide who got it.

Key terms:
- **Randomization**: assigning patients to groups by chance, so the groups end up alike in age, severity, and even factors nobody measured.
- **Control group**: patients who get standard care for comparison. Here that meant bed rest alone.
- **Blinding**: hiding group assignment from the people judging results. Chest X-rays were read by specialists who did not know which group each patient was in.

The 107 patients were young adults with severe, recently developed TB in both lungs. After six months, 4 of 55 streptomycin patients (7%) had died, compared with 14 of 52 controls (27%).

There was a catch. In many treated patients, the bacteria became **resistant** to streptomycin.
levels.college:
The MRC trial, published in the BMJ on 30 October 1948, set the template for the modern randomized controlled trial. It was run by the MRC's Streptomycin in Tuberculosis Trials Committee. Austin Bradford Hill supplied the statistical design, and clinician Marc Daniels coordinated the trial across several hospital centres.

**Design**
- **Population**: patients aged roughly 15 to 30 with acute, progressive, bilateral pulmonary TB of recent onset. All were unsuitable for collapse therapy, a technique that rested the lung by collapsing it. Restricting entry to this group made outcomes more uniform.
- **Allocation**: Hill prepared series of random sampling numbers, separate for each sex at each centre. Assignments were sealed in envelopes and opened at a central office only after a patient had been accepted into the trial. Clinicians therefore could not predict or influence group membership. This is **allocation concealment**.
- **Comparison**: streptomycin plus bed rest versus bed rest alone. There was no placebo injection.
- **Assessment**: serial chest X-rays were judged by two radiologists and a clinician working independently, unaware of allocation.

**Results at six months**
- Deaths: 7% with streptomycin versus 27% in controls.
- Considerable radiological improvement: 51% versus 8%.
- Vestibular toxicity (giddiness and balance problems) was common in treated patients.
- Streptomycin-resistant bacilli emerged in most treated patients whose cultures were tested.

**Mechanism**: streptomycin is an **aminoglycoside**. It binds the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit near the 16S rRNA decoding site, causing misreading of mRNA and faulty proteins. The effect is bactericidal.

**What came next**: the resistance problem drove a second MRC trial, published in 1950. Adding **para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS)** to streptomycin sharply reduced the emergence of resistance. This established the principle of **combination therapy** for TB, which still governs treatment today. Isoniazid followed in 1952.
levels.phd:
The trial's novelty was not the idea of a comparison group but how that comparison was protected from bias. Earlier landmarks include James Lind's 1747 scurvy experiment and Johannes Fibiger's 1898 diphtheria serum study, which allocated patients by alternate days. In 1931, Amberson's sanocrysin study in TB matched two groups and then tossed a single coin to decide which group got the gold compound. One random event at the group level does little to balance hidden prognostic factors. The MRC's 1943-44 patulin trial for the common cold used alternation with a placebo and was negative.

Hill knew alternation was predictable: a clinician who knows the next assignment can steer patients toward or away from it. Hill had set out his methods in the Lancet series that became Principles of Medical Statistics (1937). His case for randomization stressed bias prevention, not Fisher's Rothamsted-derived argument that randomization underpins valid significance tests. A concurrent MRC whooping cough vaccine trial (published 1951) also randomized, and historians debate priority.

The resistance finding has a clean quantitative explanation. Spontaneous chromosomal mutations conferring streptomycin resistance arise in roughly 1 in a million bacilli. They occur mainly in rpsL (ribosomal protein S12) and rrs (16S rRNA). A cavitary lesion can hold 10^8 or more organisms, so resistant mutants are almost certainly present before treatment, and monotherapy selects them. With two drugs, the chance of a bacillus resisting both is roughly the product of the individual frequencies, which explains the PAS result. A five-year follow-up found the mortality gap had narrowed considerably, consistent with resistance-driven relapse.

**Ethics**: no informed consent was sought by modern standards, and controls were not told they were in a trial. The justification was scarcity: the drug could not be given to everyone. Notably, patients with TB meningitis and miliary TB received streptomycin outside the trial. Untreated, these forms were almost uniformly fatal, and dramatic uncontrolled responses meant there was no genuine uncertainty, or **equipoise**, to justify randomizing them.
levels.expert:
The 1948 design anticipated features whose importance was later measured empirically. Schulz and colleagues (JAMA, 1995) analysed trials in meta-analyses and found that inadequate or unclear allocation concealment exaggerated treatment effects by roughly 30-40%. Concealment mattered more than whether the random sequence itself was well generated. Hill's sealed central envelopes had addressed the larger problem. Reporting standards such as CONSORT (1996) now require explicit description of sequence generation and concealment.

Retrospective critiques remain instructive:
- **Equipoise**: Freedman's concept of clinical equipoise (1987) asks whether the expert community is genuinely uncertain. Some US uncontrolled data already suggested benefit, so scarcity rather than uncertainty carried the ethical weight.
- **Endpoints**: radiological change is a surrogate. Mortality was decisive at six months, but durable benefit was undermined by resistance. This is a reminder that short follow-up can overstate a drug's value.
- **Small samples, big effects**: when effects are dramatic, randomization may be unnecessary. Glasziou and colleagues (BMJ, 2007) argued that very large effect sizes can be convincing without an RCT. Most real effects are modest, however, which is exactly where bias can masquerade as benefit.

The British lineage of pragmatic trials continues. The RECOVERY platform trial (2020) randomized tens of thousands of hospitalized COVID-19 patients with minimal paperwork. It showed that dexamethasone reduced mortality by about a third in ventilated patients, a direct descendant of the MRC's simple, centrally randomized approach.

TB itself has stayed a proving ground. MRC trials in East Africa, Hong Kong and Madras in the 1970s built the six-month rifampicin-based short-course regimen. More recently, Study 31/A5349 (2021) showed that a four-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen was noninferior. Nix-TB supported the bedaquiline-pretomanid-linezolid (BPaL) regimen for highly drug-resistant disease.

For a neuro-minded pharmacologist, aminoglycoside ototoxicity is a lasting lesson. Carriers of the mitochondrial MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant have a 12S rRNA that resembles the bacterial binding site, which predisposes them to profound hearing loss after exposure. CPIC guidance (2022) advises avoiding aminoglycosides in carriers when alternatives exist. Open questions include Bayesian adaptive designs and consent waivers in emergency research.

test.q: Who designed the random allocation for the 1948 streptomycin trial?
test.explain: The statistician Austin Bradford Hill designed the randomization. Fisher championed randomization in agriculture, but he did not design this trial.

test.q: Why was it considered ethical to give some patients bed rest without streptomycin?
choices: Patients had signed detailed consent forms
Bed rest was known to cure most TB cases
The drug was in short supply in Britain
Animal studies had shown the drug was useless
test.explain: Post-war Britain had too little streptomycin to treat everyone, so letting chance decide was fair. Modern informed consent was not obtained.

test.q: How were patients assigned to treatment or control?
choices: Patients choosing whether to receive the drug
Alternating patients in order of admission
Doctors picking which patients looked suitable
test.explain: Random sampling numbers were sealed in envelopes and opened centrally after enrolment. Alternation, used in earlier studies, is predictable and can be manipulated.

test.q: What did the control group receive?
test.explain: Controls received the standard care of the time, bed rest alone. There was no placebo injection, and patients were chosen because they were unsuitable for collapse therapy.

test.q: What were the six-month death rates (streptomycin group vs control group)?
test.explain: 4 of 55 streptomycin patients (7%) died, compared with 14 of 52 controls (27%).

test.q: What major problem appeared in patients treated with streptomycin?
choices: Bacteria becoming resistant to the drug
Severe allergic reactions in most patients
Many patients dropping out of the study
test.explain: Resistant TB bacilli emerged in most treated patients whose cultures were tested, which limited lasting benefit.

test.q: Which step reduced bias when judging how patients' lungs changed?
choices: Results announced to patients each month
X-rays read by experts unaware of group
Bed rest given on the same ward to both
Patients weighed weekly by their own doctors
test.explain: Radiologists and a clinician assessed the chest X-rays independently without knowing the allocation. This is blinded outcome assessment.

test.q: What is the main purpose of randomizing patients?
choices: To guarantee that the drug group improves
To make the trial cheaper to run
To balance groups, even on unmeasured traits
To let doctors give the drug to the sickest
test.explain: Chance allocation tends to balance known and unknown prognostic factors and blocks selection bias. Letting doctors choose would reintroduce bias.

test.q: Which drug was added to streptomycin in the follow-up MRC trial to reduce resistance?
test.explain: Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) combined with streptomycin sharply cut resistance. Isoniazid arrived in 1952, and rifampicin came later still.

test.q: Which lung disease did the 1948 MRC trial study?
test.explain: The trial tested streptomycin in acute, progressive pulmonary tuberculosis.

test.q: Streptomycin was isolated in 1943 from a soil bacterium of the genus ___.
test.explain: Albert Schatz, working in Selman Waksman's lab, isolated it from Streptomyces griseus.

test.q: Assigning patients to treatment groups by chance is called ___.
test.explain: Randomization prevents investigators from choosing who gets the treatment and balances groups.

advancedTest.q: Hill sealed each allocation in an envelope that was opened centrally only after a patient was enrolled. What bias does this prevent that an openly posted random list would not?
choices: Small samples giving imbalanced groups by chance
Radiologists favouring the drug on X-rays
Doctors steering patients into foreseeable groups
Patients guessing their group from side effects
advancedTest.explain: Concealment stops clinicians from foreseeing the next assignment and enrolling or excluding patients accordingly. Chance imbalance in small samples is not prevented by concealment.

advancedTest.q: The six-month mortality gap narrowed considerably by five years, and most tested treated patients grew resistant bacilli. What is the best inference?
choices: Randomization failed and groups differed at baseline
Bed rest becomes more harmful with longer follow-up
Streptomycin had no real effect at any stage of disease
Single-drug therapy selected resistant mutants over time
advancedTest.explain: Pre-existing resistant mutants in large bacillary populations are selected by monotherapy, eroding durable benefit. The early mortality difference shows the drug did work initially.

advancedTest.q: Why were patients with TB meningitis given streptomycin outside the trial instead of being randomized?
choices: Regulators barred children from drug research then
Their illness was usually too mild to need the drug
Their near-certain death without it removed equipoise
The drug was thought unable to reach the brain
advancedTest.explain: Untreated TB meningitis was almost uniformly fatal, and responses to streptomycin were dramatic. With no genuine uncertainty, withholding the drug could not be justified.

advancedTest.q: Amberson's 1931 sanocrysin study tossed one coin to decide which of two pre-matched groups received the drug. What is its key weakness relative to the MRC design?
choices: Coin tosses are less random than number tables
One coin toss does little to balance hidden factors
Matching patients first makes a trial unethical
It lacked any untreated comparison group
advancedTest.explain: A single group-level random event cannot spread unknown prognostic factors evenly. Individual randomization repeats the chance process for every patient, which is what achieves balance.

lessons.title: The Tuskegee Study and the Belmont Report

levels.kid:
Long ago, from 1932 to 1972, government doctors in Alabama studied 600 Black men. Many of them had a serious germ illness called **syphilis**.

The doctors did not tell the men the truth. They just said the men had "bad blood." Around 1947 a cure called **penicillin** became the normal treatment, but the doctors still did not give it. They only watched to see what the illness would do. That was cruel and unfair.

A worker named Peter Buxtun knew it was wrong. He told a news reporter, and the study was stopped.

Afterward, leaders wrote rules called the **Belmont Report**:
- **Respect**: tell people the truth and ask their permission.
- **Do good**: keep people safe.
- **Be fair (justice)**: don't pick only poor or powerless people.

Today a special team called an **IRB** checks every study.
levels.hs:
The **Tuskegee Study of Untreated Syphilis in the Negro Male** was run by the **US Public Health Service (PHS)** from 1932 to 1972 in Macon County, Alabama. Researchers enrolled about 600 poor Black men, mostly sharecroppers: 399 with **latent syphilis** (infection without symptoms) and 201 without it as controls. **Syphilis** is caused by the bacterium *Treponema pallidum*. Untreated, it can damage the heart, the aorta and the brain years later.

The goal was to watch the disease progress without treatment. The men were never told their diagnosis; they were told they had "bad blood." To keep them enrolled, the PHS offered free meals, rides, medical exams and **burial insurance**. By the late 1940s **penicillin** was the standard cure, yet it was withheld for 25 more years.

In 1972 PHS worker **Peter Buxtun** gave the story to Associated Press reporter Jean Heller. Public outrage ended the study. Many men had died of syphilis or its complications, some wives were infected, and children were born with congenital syphilis.

Congress passed the **National Research Act** (1974). A commission it created wrote the **Belmont Report** (1978), which set three principles for research on people:
- **Respect for persons**: informed consent.
- **Beneficence**: maximize benefits, minimize harms.
- **Justice**: share research burdens and benefits fairly.

US studies on people now need approval from an **Institutional Review Board (IRB)**.
levels.college:
The Tuskegee study was not a clinical trial. Nothing was tested and no one was randomized. It was a deliberately non-therapeutic **natural-history study** that relied on deception.

**Design and deception**
- Run by the US Public Health Service with the Tuskegee Institute, 1932 to 1972: 399 men with latent syphilis and 201 uninfected controls.
- Men were told they were being treated for "bad blood." Diagnostic **lumbar punctures**, done to look for neurosyphilis, were presented as "special free treatment."
- **Nurse Eunice Rivers**, a Black public health nurse, was the men's main contact for decades. Her trust in the community helped keep retention high.
- Autopsies were a key endpoint. Burial insurance helped secure families' consent to them.

**Withholding a cure**
Penicillin became standard therapy for syphilis by about 1947. The PHS not only withheld it but worked to stop the men getting treatment elsewhere. During World War II it gave local draft boards lists of participants so they would be excluded from the military's treatment programs. The study also ran on after the 1947 **Nuremberg Code** made voluntary consent a stated international principle.

**Exposure and aftermath**
Peter Buxtun protested inside the PHS from 1966. In July 1972 he took the story to the press. Senate hearings led by Edward Kennedy followed in 1973. Attorney Fred Gray filed a class-action suit, settled in 1974 for $10 million. The government created a health benefit program for survivors and their families. President Clinton issued a formal apology in 1997.

**The Belmont Report** set out three principles, each with a practical application:
- **Respect for persons** leads to **informed consent**: disclosure, comprehension and voluntariness. It also calls for extra protection for people with reduced autonomy.
- **Beneficence** leads to a systematic **risk-benefit assessment**.
- **Justice** leads to **fair selection of subjects**, so vulnerable groups do not carry the burdens of research while others reap the benefits.
levels.phd:
**Origins.** In 1929 to 1931 the Rosenwald Fund supported a syphilis *treatment* demonstration in the rural South. The Depression ended its funding. PHS venereal disease chief **Taliaferro Clark** then proposed a short observational study of 6 to 12 months. It was partly framed as a racial comparison with the **Oslo study** of untreated syphilis, mostly in white patients. **Raymond Vonderlehr** extended it into an open-ended study ending at autopsy. The scientific rationale was weak from the start. Many men had received some earlier arsenical or mercury treatment, which contaminated the "untreated" cohort. Controls who later became infected were moved into the syphilitic group.

**Institutional persistence.** The study outlived its changing directors. Results were published openly in medical journals over the decades, so the profession was not ignorant of it. In 1969, after Buxtun's complaints, a **CDC panel** reviewed the study and recommended continuing it. The scandal was not hidden misconduct. It was a sanctioned program that peers saw and accepted.

**Harm.** CDC figures state that by 1972, 28 men had died directly of syphilis and about 100 of related complications. Some 40 wives had been infected, and 19 children had been born with congenital syphilis.

**Context.** In 1966 **Henry Beecher** published "Ethics and Clinical Research" in the *NEJM*. It catalogued 22 ethically troubling studies in mainstream US research and showed that abuse was not limited to Nazi doctors. Many American researchers had seen the Nuremberg Code as a verdict on atrocities, not a rule for their own work.

**The National Commission** (1974 to 1978), chaired by Kenneth Ryan with philosopher Tom Beauchamp on staff, met at the Smithsonian's Belmont Conference Center in 1976. The report was issued in 1978 and published in the Federal Register in 1979. Its key moves:
- It drew a line between **research** (aimed at general knowledge) and **practice** (aimed at the individual patient).
- It tied each principle to an application.
- It made **justice** an explicit research principle.

Belmont folds avoiding harm into beneficence. By contrast, Beauchamp and Childress's *Principles of Biomedical Ethics* (1979) separates **nonmaleficence** as a fourth principle.

**Guatemala.** In 2010 historian **Susan Reverby** revealed PHS experiments in Guatemala (1946 to 1948) that deliberately infected people with sexually transmitted infections. PHS physician John Cutler worked on both projects.
levels.expert:
**Regulatory descendants.** Belmont's principles were written into **45 CFR 46**. Its core, the **Common Rule** (1991), is shared by federal agencies, and FDA has parallel rules in 21 CFR 50 and 56. The 2018 revision, effective 2019, added several requirements:
- A concise **key information** section at the start of consent forms.
- A **single IRB** for multisite federally funded studies.
- An option for **broad consent** to store specimens for future research.

These respond to evidence that long consent documents are poorly understood. Pitfalls IRBs still police:
- **Undue inducement**: rewards so attractive they distort judgment. Tuskegee's burial insurance was a lever on people with almost no options.
- **Exculpatory language** that appears to waive participants' rights.
- The **therapeutic misconception** (Appelbaum, 1982): participants believe trial procedures are chosen for their personal benefit and misread randomization and placebo.
- Disturbing **clinical equipoise** without adequate justification, meaning running a trial when experts no longer genuinely disagree about which arm is better.

**Justice reinterpreted.** Belmont's justice was first applied protectively, by shielding groups from research. This contributed to the routine exclusion of women and minorities. The **NIH Revitalization Act (1993)** required their inclusion in NIH-funded trials. **FDORA (2022)** requires sponsors to submit diversity action plans for many late-phase trials. Exclusion is now itself recognized as an injustice, because drugs reach the market with little data in the people who will use them.

**Mistrust: evidence and nuance.** Alsan and Wanamaker (2018) linked the 1972 disclosure to more medical mistrust and less healthcare use among Black men. They estimated it reduced life expectancy at 45 by roughly 1.5 years, about a third of the 1980 Black-white gap. Yet survey work shows that lower trial participation is driven heavily by structural barriers and by not being invited. Attributing it to Tuskegee alone can excuse poor recruitment practice. A persistent myth that the PHS *injected* men with syphilis is false. That happened in Guatemala, and repeating the error weakens accurate testimony.

**Open questions.** Can consent be meaningful in complex, adaptive or AI-driven trials? How should IRBs judge community-level risk in genomic research? Does community engagement, not just individual consent, need formal regulatory standing?

lessons.title: Fen-Phen and Drug-Induced Heart Valve Disease (1997)

levels.kid:
Your heart has four little doors inside it called **valves**. They open to let blood through, then snap shut so blood can't flow backward.

In the 1990s, millions of people took a pair of diet medicines nicknamed **fen-phen** to help them lose weight. Then doctors in Fargo, North Dakota, and at the Mayo Clinic noticed something strange. Some women who took fen-phen had thick, stiff heart valves that leaked.

Scientists later found out why. One of the medicines pushed a tiny "lock" on valve cells called **5-HT2B**. That lock told the cells to grow too much, like weeds on a door hinge.

In 1997 the risky part of fen-phen was taken off the shelves. Now, before a new medicine is sold, scientists check whether it turns that lock.
levels.hs:
**Fen-phen** was a popular weight-loss combination of two older drugs: **fenfluramine**, which increases the brain chemical **serotonin** and reduces appetite, and **phentermine**, an amphetamine-like stimulant. The FDA approved each drug separately but never approved them together. Doctors prescribed the pair **off-label** after a 1992 study by Michael Weintraub suggested the combination worked better than either alone. By 1996, US doctors were writing roughly 18 million prescriptions a year. That year, a related drug, **dexfenfluramine** (Redux), was also approved.

In July 1997, cardiologists at the **Mayo Clinic** (Heidi Connolly and colleagues), working with clinicians in Fargo, North Dakota, described 24 women with unusual **valvular heart disease**. Their heart valves were coated in shiny white plaques that made them stiff and leaky, a problem called **regurgitation**. Five of the women needed valve surgery. Under the microscope, the valves looked like those in **carcinoid syndrome**, a rare tumor condition in which tumors flood the blood with serotonin. That resemblance was a major clue.

On September 15, 1997, the FDA asked makers to withdraw fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine. Phentermine stayed on the market.

Fenfluramine had already been linked to a rare, often deadly lung condition, **pulmonary arterial hypertension** (high blood pressure in the lung arteries). Fen-phen became a lesson that drugs used by millions can cause rare harms that small, short trials miss.
levels.college:
**The drugs.** Fenfluramine (approved in the US in 1973) is a substituted amphetamine that acts as a **serotonin releaser**: it enters nerve terminals through the serotonin transporter (SERT) and makes the transporter run in reverse, dumping serotonin into the synapse. Appetite suppression is thought to work mainly through **5-HT2C receptors** on hypothalamic POMC neurons. Phentermine (approved 1959) releases norepinephrine. The off-label combination spread after Weintraub's 1992 trial. Dexfenfluramine, the d-enantiomer, was approved in 1996 as the first new anti-obesity drug in over two decades.

**The signal.** In 1997, Connolly and colleagues at the Mayo Clinic reported 24 women with valve disease after fen-phen use (published in NEJM that August). Key features:
- Lesions on both left-sided valves (mitral, aortic) and right-sided valves
- Glistening white plaques of myofibroblasts in a glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix, "stuck on" to otherwise intact leaflets
- Histology matching **carcinoid heart disease** and **ergot alkaloid** (methysergide, ergotamine) valvulopathy
- Eight patients also had pulmonary hypertension

The FDA then gathered echocardiograms; early reports found abnormal valves in roughly 30% of users, which led to withdrawal in September 1997.

**Why the carcinoid clue mattered.** In carcinoid syndrome, gut tumors release serotonin that reaches the right heart first. The lungs then break down much of it with monoamine oxidase, so left-sided valves are usually spared. Fenfluramine reaches all valves through the systemic circulation, which helps explain its left-sided lesions. The overlap pointed to **serotonin signaling** as the culprit.

**Lung harm.** The International Primary Pulmonary Hypertension Study (Abenhaim, 1996) linked appetite suppressants to pulmonary arterial hypertension, with risk rising sharply after more than three months of use. This echoed a 1960s European epidemic caused by **aminorex**, another anorectic drug.

**Legacy.** Fen-phen showed that pre-approval trials, which are short, small and not designed to detect valve disease, cannot catch every rare or delayed toxicity. Post-marketing surveillance and alert clinicians remain essential.
levels.phd:
**Molecular mechanism.** The decisive work came in 2000 from two groups: Rothman and colleagues (Circulation) and Fitzgerald and colleagues (Molecular Pharmacology). Both profiled fenfluramine, its metabolite **norfenfluramine** (formed by N-de-ethylation), and other serotonergic drugs across receptor panels. Fenfluramine itself is weak at most 5-HT receptors. Norfenfluramine, by contrast, is a high-affinity, high-efficacy **5-HT2B agonist**. Drugs known to cause valvulopathy (norfenfluramine, pergolide, ergotamine, and methylergonovine, the active metabolite of methysergide) shared 5-HT2B agonism. Serotonergic drugs without valve toxicity, such as SSRIs, did not. Serotonin release alone was therefore not sufficient; direct receptor agonism by a metabolite was the key.

**Signaling.** 5-HT2B is Gq/11-coupled and abundant on **valve interstitial cells**. Activation drives PLCβ, IP3/DAG and PKC, Src kinase, ERK1/2 phosphorylation, and cross-talk with **TGF-β** signaling. Quiescent interstitial cells transform into activated myofibroblasts that proliferate and lay down glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix, producing the characteristic surface plaques. Chronic serotonin infusion in rats reproduces this valvulopathy, and 5-HT2B knockout mice show embryonic cardiac defects, consistent with the receptor's mitogenic role in heart valves.

**Pulmonary vasculature.** In pulmonary arterial hypertension, both SERT-mediated serotonin uptake into smooth muscle and 5-HT2B signaling are implicated. Launay and colleagues (2002, Nature Medicine) showed that 5-HT2B-deficient mice resist hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension. Whether valve and lung toxicities share one mechanism remains debated.

**Epidemiology and controversy.** The early FDA figure of about 30% came from uncontrolled, selectively referred echocardiograms and overstated the risk. Controlled studies were more measured but confirmed it. Khan and colleagues (NEJM 1998) found FDA-defined regurgitation (mild or greater aortic, or moderate or greater mitral) in 22.7% of users versus 1.3% of controls. Other cohorts reported lower absolute rates. Across studies, risk rose with **duration of exposure**, with a clear excess after roughly three to six months. Many lesions were mild and stable, and some regressed after stopping the drug.

**Receptorome screening.** Bryan Roth's group argued that systematic profiling across hundreds of receptors (the "receptorome," via the NIMH Psychoactive Drug Screening Program) could predict such off-target toxicity before human exposure.
levels.expert:
**Pharmacovigilance lessons.** The fen-phen signal did not come from trials or spontaneous reporting algorithms. It came from an echocardiography team in Fargo who recognized an unusual pattern and took it to Mayo Clinic cardiologists. Clinicians remain primary signal detectors for rare, delayed, organ-specific toxicity. In practice, any unexplained restrictive regurgitation with thickened, retracted leaflets and preserved commissures should prompt a medication history. Commissural fusion instead points toward rheumatic disease.

**The 5-HT2B class recurs.**
- **Pergolide and cabergoline**, ergot-derived dopamine agonists for Parkinson's disease, were linked to valvulopathy in two 2007 NEJM studies (Schade; Zanettini). Pergolide was withdrawn from the US market that year. Non-ergot agonists such as pramipexole lack 5-HT2B agonism.
- **Benfluorex** (Mediator), a fenfluramine relative metabolized to norfenfluramine, stayed on the French market until 2009. Pulmonologist Irène Frachon's case work exposed it. Later estimates attributed hundreds to around 2,000 deaths to it, prompting overhaul of French drug regulation.

**Drug discovery practice.** 5-HT2B is now a standard safety counterscreen. A common pitfall is relying on binding data alone. Many 5-HT2B ligands are **antagonists** and appear harmless to valves, so functional agonist assays (calcium flux, IP accumulation, ERK activation) are required. Major **metabolites** must be screened too, since the parent fenfluramine was a weak agonist. **Lorcaserin**, a 5-HT2C-selective agonist designed to spare 5-HT2B, was approved for obesity in 2012. It showed no clear valve signal but was withdrawn in 2020 after an imbalance in cancer cases in the CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 trial. Solving one liability does not establish overall safety.

**Repurposing.** Fenfluramine returned in 2020 as Fintepla for seizures in **Dravet syndrome**, and in 2022 for **Lennox-Gastaut syndrome**. Its antiseizure action likely involves serotonergic and sigma-1 receptor effects. Approval came with a REMS program requiring serial echocardiograms. Valvulopathy has not been reported in trials so far, but cohorts are small and follow-up is limited, so long-term surveillance continues.

**Open questions.** Why only a minority of exposed patients develop lesions (genetics, metabolism, exposure duration) is unresolved. Biased agonism at 5-HT2B is under study, as is whether 5-HT2B antagonists could treat valve disease or pulmonary hypertension. The legal aftermath was also vast: American Home Products (Wyeth) faced a 1999 class settlement of about $3.75 billion, with eventual costs often cited near $21 billion.

lessons.title: Terfenadine, QT Prolongation and the hERG Lesson

levels.kid:
Your heart beats because of tiny electric signals. After each beat, the heart has to "reset," a bit like a drum that must stop shaking before you hit it again.

In the 1980s, a popular allergy pill called **terfenadine** helped people stop sneezing without making them sleepy. But in a few people, it slowed down the heart's reset. When the reset takes too long, the heart can wobble into a dangerous, messy rhythm.

Scientists found the problem: the pill was blocking a tiny doorway in heart cells called **hERG**. This doorway lets the heart reset.

Now, every new medicine is checked to see if it blocks the hERG doorway, so this mistake is caught early.
levels.hs:
**Terfenadine** (brand name Seldane) was approved in the United States in 1985 as one of the first **non-sedating antihistamines**, meaning it treated hay fever without the drowsiness of older drugs. It became hugely popular.

By around 1990, doctors reported cases of fainting and sudden cardiac death. The culprit was a dangerous heart rhythm called **torsades de pointes** (French for "twisting of the points"), which can turn into ventricular fibrillation.

Key terms:
- The **ECG** (electrocardiogram) records the heart's electrical activity.
- The **QT interval** is the time from the start of ventricular depolarization (the Q wave) to the end of the heart's electrical recovery (repolarization). A longer QT means slower recovery.
- **QT prolongation** raises the risk of torsades.

The problem was mostly **drug interactions**. Terfenadine is normally broken down almost completely by the liver enzyme **CYP3A4** into **fexofenadine**, a safe active form. When people also took CYP3A4 blockers such as **ketoconazole** (an antifungal), **erythromycin** (an antibiotic), or even lots of grapefruit juice, terfenadine built up in the blood.

Unchanged terfenadine blocks a potassium channel called **hERG**, which helps heart cells repolarize. Blocking it lengthens the QT interval. The FDA proposed removing terfenadine in 1997, and it left the US market in 1998. It was replaced by fexofenadine (Allegra), which doesn't block hERG meaningfully.
levels.college:
Terfenadine's story shows how a drug can be safe on its own yet dangerous in combination, and how one ion channel became the center of cardiac safety testing.

**Pharmacokinetics.** Terfenadine is a **prodrug** with extensive first-pass metabolism: CYP3A4 in the gut wall and liver converts nearly all of it to **fexofenadine** (terfenadine carboxylate), which carries the antihistamine effect. Normally, parent terfenadine in plasma is barely detectable. CYP3A4 inhibition (ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin, clarithromycin) or liver disease lets parent drug accumulate. Studies by Honig and colleagues (1993) showed ketoconazole co-administration produced measurable terfenadine levels and QT prolongation.

**Electrophysiology.** The ventricular action potential plateau ends when potassium currents repolarize the cell. A key one is the **rapid delayed rectifier current, I_Kr**, carried by channels whose pore-forming subunit is encoded by **KCNH2**, the *human ether-à-go-go-related gene* (**hERG**). Blocking I_Kr:
- Prolongs action potential duration, and therefore the QT interval
- Promotes **early afterdepolarizations (EADs)**, often via L-type calcium channel reactivation
- Increases **dispersion of repolarization** across the ventricular wall, a substrate for re-entrant torsades de pointes

**The pattern repeats.** Terfenadine wasn't unique. Withdrawals or major restrictions for hERG-related torsades include:
- **Astemizole** (antihistamine, 1999)
- **Cisapride** (gastric motility drug, 2000)
- **Grepafloxacin** (fluoroquinolone antibiotic, 1999)
- **Sertindole** (antipsychotic, suspended in 1998)

**Regulatory response.** This cluster led to the 2005 ICH guidelines: **S7B** (nonclinical testing, including hERG assays) and **E14** (the clinical "thorough QT" study). QT is corrected for heart rate, giving **QTc**, typically with Bazett's or Fridericia's formula.

**Fexofenadine** is the lesson's success: it's the active metabolite, it barely blocks hERG, and it's polar enough to stay out of the brain, so it remains non-sedating.
levels.phd:
**Why hERG is promiscuous.** Unlike most potassium channels, hERG binds a remarkably diverse range of drugs. Mutagenesis work by Mitcheson, Sanguinetti and colleagues (2000) located the binding site in the inner cavity. Aromatic residues **Tyr652** and **Phe656** on the S6 helices, along with pore-helix residues such as Thr623 and Ser624, form a large hydrophobic vestibule. Two features of hERG are thought to explain its size: it lacks the Pro-X-Pro motif that kinks S6 in Kv channels, and the cavity is unusually wide. A common blocker pharmacophore emerged: a basic, protonatable nitrogen with flanking lipophilic aromatic groups. Terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride and many antipsychotics fit it. Cryo-EM structures of hERG (Wang & MacKinnon, 2017) confirmed a central cavity with small hydrophobic side pockets.

**State dependence and trapping.** Many blockers enter only when the channel is open or inactivated, and some become trapped behind the closing gate. This affects how much block accumulates at different heart rates. hERG's fast C-type inactivation gives it its inward rectification, and drug affinity often depends on inactivation.

**Genetic parallel.** Loss-of-function KCNH2 mutations cause congenital **long QT syndrome type 2 (LQT2)**, identified by Curran, Keating and colleagues (1995). Sanguinetti's group showed the same year that hERG encodes I_Kr. Drug-induced and inherited LQTS converge on the same current. Roden's concept of **repolarization reserve** explains why only some patients develop torsades: redundant currents (I_Ks, encoded by KCNQ1/KCNE1) normally compensate. These can be reduced by hypokalemia, bradycardia, female sex, structural heart disease, or subclinical channel variants. These make the system fragile.

**Nuance: hERG is not destiny.** Some drugs block hERG potently but cause little torsades. **Verapamil** is the classic example, because simultaneous L-type calcium block suppresses EADs. **Ranolazine** is a related case: it prolongs QT modestly, but its late sodium current block appears protective. Conversely, QT prolongation is an imperfect surrogate. **Amiodarone** markedly prolongs QT yet rarely causes torsades, likely because it blocks several channels and causes relatively uniform repolarization. The margin between free plasma concentration and hERG IC50 matters more than IC50 alone. A ratio of ~30-fold was proposed by Redfern and colleagues (2003) as a rough safety benchmark.
levels.expert:
**Consequences of the S7B/E14 era.** The 2005 framework succeeded: since then, essentially no new drug has been withdrawn for unanticipated torsades. But it was blunt. A hERG hit or a positive thorough QT (TQT) study often ended a compound's development, even though many hERG blockers are clinically benign. The E14 regulatory threshold was an upper 95% confidence bound for the placebo-corrected mean QTc change exceeding 10 ms. This prioritized sensitivity over specificity. It probably discarded useful molecules and pushed medicinal chemists toward reflexive tactics: lowering basicity (pKa), reducing lipophilicity, or adding carboxylic acids. Fexofenadine is the natural template for that last approach.

**CiPA and the 2022 update.** The FDA-led **Comprehensive in vitro Proarrhythmia Assay** initiative (launched 2013) reframed the question from "does it prolong QT?" to "is it proarrhythmic?" Its components:
- Patch-clamp profiling across multiple cardiac currents (hERG, Cav1.2, Nav1.5 peak and late, and others)
- In silico modeling of a human ventricular myocyte (a modified O'Hara-Rudy model), producing a torsades risk metric
- Confirmation in **human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes**
- Clinical ECG analysis including **J-Tpeak**. Pure hERG block lengthens it, whereas added late-sodium or calcium block does not.

The 2022 **ICH E14/S7B Q&As** formally integrated nonclinical data, allowing a negative integrated risk assessment to substitute for some TQT findings. **Concentration-QTc modeling** from intensively sampled phase 1 studies (Darpo et al., the IQ-CSRC study, 2015) has largely replaced dedicated TQT trials.

**Clinical pitfalls that persist:**
- Bazett's correction overcorrects at high heart rates, which falsely lengthens QTc in tachycardic patients. Fridericia's formula is preferred in trials.
- Torsades risk is typically multifactorial: an added CYP3A4 inhibitor, hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, diuretics, bradycardia, and congenital variants. The CredibleMeds lists (Woosley) help stratify drugs.
- Methadone, haloperidol (intravenous), ondansetron, citalopram and fluoroquinolones remain in wide use. They are managed with ECG monitoring rather than banned.

**Open questions:** how to validate CiPA prospectively for novel modalities, how to handle drug-induced hERG *trafficking* defects. Pentamidine and arsenic trioxide, for example, reduce surface channel expression rather than blocking the pore, and acute patch-clamp assays miss this. Polygenic risk scores for drug-induced LQTS might eventually personalize prescribing.

lessons.title: TGN1412: The 2006 First-in-Human Trial Disaster

levels.kid:
Before a new medicine is given to sick people, it is tested on a few healthy volunteers first. This is called a **first-in-human** trial.

In March 2006, in London, six healthy young men got a new medicine called **TGN1412**. It was made to switch on helper cells in the immune system, the body's army against germs.

But it switched on far too many soldiers at once. Imagine every fire alarm in a city ringing together. The men's bodies flooded with alarm signals called **cytokines**. Within hours they became very sick, and their organs began to fail.

Doctors in intensive care saved all six. Afterward, scientists changed the rules. Now new medicines like this start with much smaller amounts, and volunteers get them one at a time.
levels.hs:
On 13 March 2006, eight healthy men joined a **first-in-human** (Phase I) trial at Northwick Park Hospital in London. Six received **TGN1412**, an experimental drug made by the German company TeGenero. Two got a **placebo**, a dummy treatment.

TGN1412 was a **monoclonal antibody**, a lab-made protein that sticks to one specific target. Its target was **CD28**, a switch on **T cells**, which are white blood cells that direct immune attacks. Normally a T cell needs two signals to activate. TGN1412 was a **superagonist**, meaning it could turn T cells on through CD28 alone. The hope was to boost helpful regulatory T cells and treat diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and leukemia.

Within about 90 minutes, all six men who got the drug developed headaches, back pain, fever and falling blood pressure. Their immune cells released a flood of signaling proteins called **cytokines**. This is a **cytokine storm** (now called **cytokine release syndrome**). Several needed ventilators and dialysis. All six survived, but some suffered lasting harm, including the loss of fingers and toes in one man.

The drug had seemed safe in monkeys at far higher amounts. The disaster showed that animal tests can miss human-specific dangers. It led to new rules: dose new volunteers one at a time, and choose starting doses based on the drug's biological effect, not just on animal toxicity.
levels.college:
**The trial.** The TGN1412 Phase I study (Parexel, at Northwick Park, March 2006) gave the antibody to six volunteers within roughly ten minutes of each other. All six developed **cytokine release syndrome (CRS)** and multi-organ failure. All survived after intensive care.

**The molecule.** TGN1412 (later TAB08) is a humanized **IgG4** monoclonal antibody against **CD28**, the main costimulatory receptor on T cells. Ordinary T-cell activation needs:
- **Signal 1**: the T-cell receptor (TCR)/CD3 recognizing antigen on MHC
- **Signal 2**: CD28 binding B7 ligands (CD80/CD86)

Conventional anti-CD28 antibodies bind near the ligand site. **Superagonists** bind the laterally exposed C"D loop of CD28's extracellular domain. This lets them crosslink receptors and activate T cells without Signal 1. In rodents, the parent antibody (JJ316) mainly expanded **regulatory T cells (Tregs)**, which suggested therapeutic immunosuppression.

**What happened.** Volunteers released large amounts of TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-6 and IL-10. Blood lymphocytes and monocytes fell sharply within hours. The clinical picture was hypotension, capillary leak, acute lung injury, renal failure and coagulopathy. Later, ischemic damage to the fingers and toes appeared.

**Why preclinical tests missed it.** Cynomolgus macaques tolerated much higher doses without a cytokine storm, even though TGN1412 bound macaque CD28. Later work identified a key reason: macaque CD4+ effector memory T cells lose CD28 expression, while human ones keep it.

**Regulatory response.** The Duff Report (2006) and EMA guidance (2007, revised 2017) introduced:
- **Sentinel dosing**: one or two subjects first, with gaps between subjects
- Choosing the starting dose from the **MABEL** (Minimal Anticipated Biological Effect Level), not only from animal toxicity
- Special caution for agonists, immune targets and molecules with species-specific biology
- Trial sites with immediate access to intensive care
levels.phd:
**Starting dose logic.** The volunteers' starting dose was chosen from a macaque NOAEL by allometric scaling with a safety factor, the standard FDA approach based on human-equivalent dose. Retrospective MABEL analysis told a different story. In vitro and receptor-occupancy data implied this dose saturated most CD28 at peak. The biologically minimal dose was estimated to be several hundredfold lower. The study population received a near-maximal pharmacological effect, not a sub-pharmacological probe. Toxicity-based scaling suits drugs whose harm tracks overall exposure. It fails for high-affinity immune agonists, where harm tracks how much of the target is occupied.

**Mechanism.** CD28 superagonism needs FcγR-mediated crosslinking or high-density presentation. TGN1412 caused little response in standard soluble-phase PBMC assays, which falsely reassured investigators. Stebbings et al. (NIBSC, 2007) showed robust cytokine release when the antibody was immobilized on plastic, either air-dried or wet-coated. Römer et al. (2011) found that culturing PBMCs at high density beforehand restored responses in suspension. That pre-culture resets T cells to a tissue-like, primed state. Eastwood et al. (2010) pinned the main source of cytokines on human CD4+ effector memory T cells. Macaque CD4+ effector memory cells lack CD28, so no matching cell population existed in the animal model. Because the antibody is IgG4, Fc-dependent effects were expected to be minimal. Even so, tissue FcγR-bearing cells likely provided the crosslinking.

**Lymphocyte trafficking.** The deep drop in circulating lymphocytes within hours reflects margination and tissue homing of activated cells, not just their death. This likely contributed to endothelial injury and capillary leak.

**Nuance.** The Tregs-first paradigm came from rats and held in vivo there. Human data showed that effector memory cells dominate the acute response. A species difference in a costimulatory receptor reversed the drug's overall effect.

**Postscript.** TheraMAB later re-tested the molecule as TAB08 in Russia. It started at roughly a thousandth of the 2006 dose. That dose produced Treg-skewed effects without CRS, consistent with MABEL logic. TeGenero went insolvent in 2006.
levels.expert:
**Clinical course.** Investigators at first read the early rigors and pain as infusion reactions. Corticosteroids and anti-IL-2R antibody (daclizumab) were given only after deterioration. Hours later, transfer to intensive care brought ventilation, hemofiltration and vasopressors. Suntharalingam et al. (NEJM 2006) documented early profound lymphopenia and a cytokine profile that predated modern CRS grading. Today the response would include the IL-6 receptor blocker **tocilizumab**. That use was validated later in CAR-T therapy, where CRS is now graded by ASTCT consensus criteria. Late effects in some volunteers included digital gangrene and persistent immune abnormalities.

**Design lessons beyond MABEL.**
- **Dosing interval**: giving drug to subjects about ten minutes apart left no time to see the first reaction. Observation windows should match the expected pharmacodynamic onset.
- **Assays must reproduce the in vivo condition.** Cytokine release assays now pair immobilized or high-density formats with whole-blood tests. Even so, no format reliably predicts CRS for every antibody. Positive controls such as OKT3 (anti-CD3) are essential.
- **Pick species by matching pharmacology, not just target binding.** Binding the target does not mean the animal's cells respond the same way. Humanized mice and human primary cell systems help fill the gap.
- **Risk factors**: agonists, signal amplification (cascades, receptor clustering), pleiotropic immune targets and long half-lives call for dose escalation designed with PK/PD modeling.

**Enduring relevance.** Bispecific T-cell engagers, CD28 costimulatory bispecifics and IL-2 variants re-raise these exact problems. Some CD28 bispecifics now under study are built to activate only when a tumor antigen is bound. These conditional designs aim to avoid systemic superagonism. Debate continues about how far MABEL should go. Starting too low can leave patients in oncology first-in-human trials on ineffective doses. Pharmacologically active dose (PAD) approaches try to balance safety against benefit.

**Open questions.** Can a human ex vivo system serve as the decision-making species for immune agonists? How much tissue FcγR crosslinking explains the reaction compared with the antibody's own molecular properties? For a neurosurgery-minded student, the parallel is clear. Intrathecal and CNS-directed immunotherapies face the same first-dose uncertainty, as with CAR-T neurotoxicity (ICANS).

keyPoints: In March 2006 six healthy volunteers got TGN1412 and developed life-threatening cytokine storm
TGN1412 was a CD28 superagonist antibody that activated T cells without the TCR signal
Macaques missed the danger partly because their effector memory T cells lack CD28
The starting dose came from animal toxicity scaling, not the minimal biological effect
Reforms: MABEL-based starting doses and sentinel dosing one subject at a time
Cytokine release assays must mimic in vivo conditions such as immobilized antibody

test.q: What was the molecular target of TGN1412?
test.explain: TGN1412 bound CD28, the main costimulatory receptor on T cells. CD3 is part of the TCR complex, a different signal.

test.q: What made TGN1412 a superagonist?
choices: It killed regulatory T cells selectively
It bound antigen presented on MHC directly
It activated T cells without a TCR signal
It blocked costimulation from B7 ligands
test.explain: Superagonists bind CD28's C"D loop and can activate T cells through CD28 alone, bypassing Signal 1.

test.q: The syndrome the volunteers developed is best called:
test.explain: A massive release of TNF-α, IL-6, IFN-γ and other cytokines defines cytokine release syndrome (cytokine storm).

test.q: Why did macaque studies fail to predict the reaction?
choices: Macaque effector memory T cells lack CD28
Macaque CD28 did not bind TGN1412
test.explain: TGN1412 bound macaque CD28, but macaque CD4+ effector memory cells, the main cytokine source in humans, do not express CD28.

test.q: What does MABEL stand for?
test.explain: MABEL bases the starting dose on the smallest expected biological effect, not on animal toxicity alone.

test.q: Which trial design flaw made the 2006 disaster worse?
choices: The drug was taken by mouth
The trial had no placebo group
Patients rather than volunteers were enrolled
test.explain: All six were dosed about ten minutes apart, so the first reaction could not warn investigators. Sentinel dosing fixes this.

test.q: Initial lab cytokine release assays were reassuring mainly because:
choices: The cells came from macaque donors
The assays measured just one cytokine
The antibody was in soluble form
test.explain: Soluble TGN1412 caused little response. Immobilized antibody or high-density pre-cultured cells revealed strong cytokine release.

test.q: The rodent parent antibody suggested TGN1412 would mainly expand:
test.explain: In rats, CD28 superagonists preferentially expanded Tregs, suggesting a use in autoimmune disease.

test.q: Which reform followed the TGN1412 trial?
choices: Testing new drugs on patients before volunteers
Sentinel dosing of single subjects first
Replacing animal studies with placebo arms
test.explain: Guidance from the Duff Report and EMA introduced sentinel dosing and MABEL-based starting doses.

test.q: TGN1412 is a monoclonal ___ against CD28.
test.explain: It was a humanized IgG4 monoclonal antibody.

test.q: What type of white blood cell does CD28 sit on and help activate?
test.explain: CD28 is a costimulatory receptor on T lymphocytes.

test.q: The TGN1412 trial took place at ___ Park Hospital in London.
test.explain: The Phase I unit at Northwick Park Hospital ran the March 2006 trial.

kidTest.q: Who gets a new medicine first in a first-in-human trial?
kidTest.explain: A few healthy volunteers usually try it first.

kidTest.q: What part of the body did TGN1412 switch on?
kidTest.explain: It switched on immune helper cells, the body's army.

kidTest.q: What went wrong?
choices: Too many immune cells switched on at once
The volunteers fell asleep for days
kidTest.explain: Too many immune cells turned on and released too many alarm signals.

kidTest.q: What changed afterward?
choices: Trials now give the biggest amounts first
Volunteers now get new medicines one at a time
Medicines are now tested on monkeys instead
kidTest.explain: Now new medicines like this start small, and volunteers get them one by one.

kidTest.q: The alarm signals the body made are called c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Cytokines are the immune system's signaling messages.

advancedTest.q: Why did NOAEL-based allometric scaling fail for TGN1412 specifically?
choices: Harm tracked target occupancy, near-saturated at that dose
Allometric scaling overestimated human body surface area
Its IgG4 format made it build up in human kidney tissue
Its human half-life was far shorter than its macaque half-life
advancedTest.explain: For high-affinity immune agonists, harm follows pharmacology. The chosen dose saturated most CD28, so MABEL would have picked a far lower dose.

advancedTest.q: Immobilized TGN1412 triggered cytokines in vitro, but soluble antibody did not. What does this imply about in vivo activity?
choices: Soluble antibody was degraded before it could reach T cells
Cytokines came mainly from monocytes activated by plastic
The antibody acted mainly through complement-dependent lysis
Tissue crosslinking, e.g. by FcγR-bearing cells, enabled it
advancedTest.explain: Superagonism needs crosslinking or high-density presentation. In vivo, cell-surface FcγRs probably provided this, despite the IgG4 format.

advancedTest.q: A new T-cell agonist binds monkey and human targets equally. What is the strongest remaining concern?
choices: Target expression on responding subsets may differ by species
Human trials detect cytokine release too late to matter
Binding affinity will drop sharply once diluted in human plasma
Monkeys clear antibodies mainly through liver enzymes
advancedTest.explain: TGN1412 showed that equal binding can hide species differences in which cells express the target, as with CD28 on effector memory cells.

advancedTest.q: TAB08 at a far lower starting dose produced Treg-skewed effects without CRS. This most supports:
choices: Dose-dependent selectivity favoring Tregs at low occupancy
Full species equivalence between rodent and human T cells
Human effector memory T cells lacking CD28 expression
IgG4 antibodies being inherently free of cytokine risk
advancedTest.explain: Low occupancy may favor Treg responses, while high occupancy recruits effector memory cells. This fits MABEL logic.
